‎Once again, Africa’s effort to lift itself from the world’s distribution of power established in 1945, which seems to limit the continent’s influence on the global scene, ended in futility last September.
‎Despite rallying each other and presenting one front, African countries could not convince the world for, at least, a permanent seat on the UN Security Council, a sad development that leaves the continent still tied to the 81-year-old global distribution of power.
‎Nigeria, which led the move at the General Debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, United States of America, was very clear and vehement on Africa’s demand: two permanent seats, with veto power, and five non-permanent ones.
‎The continent also demanded for reforms at the UN body, starting with an amendment to the charter amongst others that are skewed against Africa.
‎The demands are also in line with the African Union’s unified position on the issue as captured by the Ezulwini Consensus of 2025 and the Sirte Declaration.
‎But observers are wondering the import of the permanent seats and all the efforts being made to get them.
‎Some query what the continent will gain from getting permanent seats at the UN Security Council as the United States of America, France, United Kingdom, Russia and China; the five permanent members, still have their challenges despite having veto powers.

‎According to Samuel Onikoyi, a Nigerian academic in Brussels, the continent should rather request for the collapsing of the permanent membership structure than demanding for seats.
‎“With the way global politics is being played, I don’t see the five permanent members allowing reforms for more members to join them on the permanent seat. Even if that will happen, not an African country for now, because of the perception of Africa as poor, hungry and aids-seeking continent,” he said.
‎Onikoyi, a researcher, also noted that Africa does not have what it takes to play in the global security scene as the world still see it as a continent battling for survival.
‎“When the UN Security Council was established in 1945, Africa was under colonial rule. But having gained independence decades after, many had expected the continent to show strength in political, technological, socio-economic and infrastructural advancements. But we keep lagging and that speaks against us even at the UN today,” Onikoyi said.
‎Nuhu Yari, a lawyer and an international affairs expert, decried that the country cannot count for what it gained for the five times Nigeria was a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council.
‎“We are busy lobbying for permanent seats, but what have we really gained from the five times we got closer to that seat. Every representation should boil down to the welfare of the citizens,” Yari said.
‎The Kaduna-based lawyer decried Nigerian cannot point to what it has gained from being members of ECOWAS and AU when its citizens are being treated badly even in Africa, hence demand for permanent seat on the UN Security Council should come with direct benefits for the citizens, else it should be jettisoned.
‎But Kazeem Fadahunsi, a university don and security strategist, argued that even if Africa is to be considered for the permanent seats, countries like Egypt and South Africa may be favoured because they understand international politics better than Nigeria.
‎“I have followed global politics and power for close to five decades and I have discovered that it is all about vested interests, blocs and suppression. Africa is not there at all and is being suppressed. We need to up our game starting with rejecting foreign aids, fighting corruption, addressing hunger and poverty challenges and then taking good shots at technological development,” he said.
‎Speaking further, he noted that some powerful countries do not see the need to be on the security council today because they can hold on their own.
‎“Are Germany, Japan, South Korea, Brazil, Canada, Spain and even Turkey not good and strong enough to have permanent seats on the UN Security Council?
‎“I think they have moved on beyond the seats to create empires and blocs for themselves, which the five countries on the permanent seats also recognise today.
‎“Africa should put its house in order, settle issues that make the world to look down on it, gain respect and move on. That is what should matter for Africa and not necessarily permanent seats,” he said.
‎For those who argue that Africa needs to get the seats because of its huge population and 54 countries, Fadahunsi noted that Brazil in South America and India in Asia are more populous than any African country, yet they do not occupy permanent seats.
‎But some counter the above, insisting that the continent and Nigeria in particular, has more to gain from being on the permanent seat of the UN Security Council.
‎According to Fola Aina, faculty member, School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), London, being on the permanent seat is significant for any African country.
‎For Nigeria, Aina, who doubles as a political scientist and international security expert, noted that the position would enhance the country’s global rating and influence.
‎Speaking further, he explained that the permanent seats will give Africa prominence in international security decisions, while also boosting Nigeria’s position in ECOWAS and Africa at large as a regional influence and power.
‎Speaking from an insider view, Ibrahim Gambari, a professor and former Nigerian permanent representative to the UN, noted that the country has a lot to gain from being on the permanent seat.
‎According to him, one cannot be a candidate of the Secretary-General of UN unless each of the five permanent members agree, which implies gain from huge influence on global affairs.
‎For Gambari, Nigeria’s former Minister of Foreign Affairs, there is a lot to gain given the continent’s size and the amount of Security Council business involving it.
‎Considering that Africa has the largest single bloc, and yet has no permanent seat on the Security Council, he decried that Africa’s absence is difficult to justify and also affects the council’s day-to-day work.
‎Nigeria and other African countries’ push for the permanent seats, according to him, are not out of place as all Security Council missions to Africa, especially peacekeeping missions, are not led by Africans.

‎The above anomaly, he noted, makes it difficult for the parties in dispute to have confidence in the Security Council team, which is often dominated by foreigners.
‎Amedu Ba, a Senegalese diplomat, also noted that with African representatives in the permanent seat category, the continent will have a sense of belonging and would be able to partake in drafting resolutions that affect her people.
‎Ba, whose diplomatic career spans the ECOWAS, AU and other affiliate bodies, disclosed that permanent seats for Africa and other unrepresented continents on the Security Council would correct the anomaly of only five countries on the seats, having veto power and being the penholders that have been drafting all the resolutions since 1945.
“The five countries occupying the permanent seats are not ready to welcome others and are also the ones drafting resolutions that run the world today. But that will change when African countries’ and others sit on the Security Council,” he said.
‎With the UK, France and Russia representing Europe, China representing Asia, and the United States of America representing North America, Ba noted that offering other continents such as Africa, South America and Australia seat in the Security Council would balance representation and boost fair play.
‎As well, Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General, also supported the call for more seats for others in the Security Council.
‎In his address at the General Assembly last September, Guterres renewed his call for Security Council reform, saying that it must become more representative and better reflect today’s geopolitical realities.
‎Sadly, he did not speak the mind of the five countries occupying the permanent seats and his call may have fallen on deaf ears.
‎President Bola Tinubu, who was represented at the General Assembly by Kashim Shettima, his vice; John Mahama, Ghanaian president and other African leaders at the global gathering, also shared the views of UN secretary-general. ‎“Security Council reform is not a favour to Africa; it is an imperative for the legitimacy, credibility and survival of the United Nations”, Mahama said.
‎President Tinubu also insisted that the world’s distribution of power established in 1945 does not hold much in 2026 for Africa and the world, hence the need for urgent reforms.
‎That need has made Nigeria to keep pushing for reforms and permanent seats for Africa at almost every UN General Assembly. Nigeria has been very vocal on the demand for a long time now and in recent times, at the 79th, 80th and this year’s 81st General Assembly.
‎But while the efforts seem elusive pursuits, many urged Africa and particularly Nigeria, to channel the efforts at solving internal challenges such as poverty, huge infrastructure deficit, corruption, insecurity and poor governance.
‎”Many countries in the world today careless about the permanent seats because they are doing well. What will the seats do for Japan, South Korea or Germany when they are very advanced in development, standard of living is very high, their people are happy, and economy booms,” Onikoyi said, while urging Africa to wake up to that reality.
‎According to him, securing the permanent seat will not stop corruption in Nigeria, it will not address poverty and will also not stop the killing of innocent people.
‎While the demand is right, Ali Bukar Fatoma, an engineer and public commentator, fears that the competition among major African states over which countries should occupy permanent seats may undermine a common position for the quest. ‎
As well, he insisted that securing permanent Security Council seats should not be regarded as the final measure of Africa’s advancement. ‎”A veto cannot substitute for industrialization, scientific achievement, reliable infrastructure, strong institutions or economic competitiveness. ‎Africa must pursue representation and transformation simultaneously. The continent should continue demanding reform because equitable representation in the world’s principal security institution is justified. ‎”At the same time, African countries must accelerate industrialisation, technological innovation, agricultural modernisation, mineral beneficiation, education, research and institutional development,” he urged. ‎
All the same, the Nigerian president thinks that the country deserves a seat on the Security Council, citing the country’s peacekeeping efforts in Africa as a model.
The nation, according to Mr. President, stands ready to take on greater responsibility and sacrifice to restore peace across the continent, just as it did in Liberia, Sierra Leone, Darfur, Mali, and The Gambia, where it committed personnel and resources when global solidarity demanded action. ‎
